maximum-depth-of-binary-tree.pattern: Tree DFS returning a value up (depth = 1 + max of the children's depths)

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.idea: The depth of a tree is one more than the deeper of its two subtrees; an empty tree has depth 0.
steps: If `root` is null, return 0.
Return `1 + max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right))`.
approaches.why: Every node is visited once. The recursion stack is as deep as the tree height h: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) for a chain.

approaches.name: Level-order BFS, counting levels
approaches.idea: Process the tree one level at a time with a queue; the number of levels is the depth. No recursion, so a very deep tree cannot overflow the call stack.
steps: If `root` is null, return 0. Put `root` in a queue; `depth = 0`.
While the queue is not empty: take exactly the nodes currently in it (one level), adding their children.
Increase `depth` after each level; return it.
approaches.why: Every node is enqueued once. The queue holds at most one level, whose size w can be up to about n/2 in a full tree.

approaches.name: Serialise both trees and compare the strings
approaches.idea: Write each tree as a preorder string that includes a marker for every missing child. Two trees are the same exactly when their strings are equal.
steps: Serialise a tree: for null write `#`, otherwise write the value, then serialise left and right, separated by commas.
Serialise `p` and `q`.
Return whether the two strings are equal.
approaches.why: Both trees are walked fully even if they differ at the root, and both strings are stored. The null markers matter: without them `[1,2]` and `[1,null,2]` would look the same.

approaches.name: Recursive comparison
approaches.idea: Two trees are the same if both are empty, or both roots exist with equal values and their left subtrees and right subtrees are the same.
steps: If both are null, return true; if exactly one is null, return false.
If the values differ, return false.
Return `same(p.left, q.left) && same(p.right, q.right)`.
approaches.why: It stops at the first difference, so it visits at most the smaller tree. The stack is as deep as the tree height.

invert-binary-tree.pattern: Tree DFS (or BFS) visiting every node once and swapping its children

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.idea: Mirroring a tree means mirroring both subtrees and swapping them.
steps: If `root` is null, return null.
Invert the left and right subtrees.
Swap `root.left` and `root.right`; return `root`.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; the stack is as deep as the tree height h.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS with a queue
approaches.idea: The order in which nodes are visited does not matter: every node just needs its children swapped once. A queue visits them all without recursion.
steps: If `root` is null, return it. Put `root` in a queue.
Pop a node, swap its children, and push the non-null children.
Repeat until the queue is empty; return `root`.
approaches.why: Each node is processed once; the queue holds at most one level (width w).

symmetric-tree.pattern: Mirror DFS: compare left.left with right.right and left.right with right.left

approaches.name: Build a mirrored copy and compare
approaches.idea: A tree is symmetric when it equals its own mirror image. Build a mirrored copy, then check the two trees are the same.
steps: Build `mirror(t)`: a new node with the same value, whose left is `mirror(t.right)` and right is `mirror(t.left)`.
Compare `root` and `mirror(root)` with the Same Tree check.
approaches.why: The copy has n new nodes; the comparison is O(n).

approaches.name: Compare the two halves as mirror images
approaches.idea: The left and right subtrees mirror each other when their roots are equal, the outer children mirror each other (`a.left` with `b.right`), and the inner children do (`a.right` with `b.left`).
steps: `mirror(a, b)`: if both are null, true; if one is null, false.
Return `a.val == b.val && mirror(a.left, b.right) && mirror(a.right, b.left)`.
Answer `mirror(root.left, root.right)`.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once with no copy; only the recursion stack (height h) is used.

path-sum.pattern: Top-down DFS carrying the remaining sum

approaches.name: Collect every root-to-leaf sum
approaches.idea: Walk the tree recording the sum of every root-to-leaf path, then check whether `targetSum` is among them.
steps: DFS carrying the running sum; at a leaf, append the sum to a list.
Return whether `targetSum` is in the list (false for an empty tree).
approaches.why: Every node is visited, and the list can hold up to about n/2 leaf sums even when the first path already matches.

approaches.name: DFS subtracting as you go
approaches.idea: Pass down how much is still needed. At a leaf, the path works exactly when the remainder equals the leaf's value. Return as soon as one path works.
steps: If `root` is null, return false.
If `root` is a leaf, return `root.val == targetSum`.
Otherwise return `hasPathSum(left, targetSum − root.val) || hasPathSum(right, targetSum − root.val)`.
approaches.why: Each node at most once, stopping early on success; only the recursion stack is used.

balanced-binary-tree.pattern: Bottom-up DFS returning height, with −1 meaning "already unbalanced"

approaches.name: Top-down: compute heights at every node
approaches.idea: Check the definition directly: at each node, compute both subtree heights from scratch and compare them, then check both subtrees the same way.
steps: `height(t)` = 0 for null, else `1 + max(height(left), height(right))`.
`isBalanced(t)`: true for null; otherwise `|height(left) − height(right)| <= 1` and both subtrees are balanced.
approaches.why: Each node's height is recomputed once for every ancestor: O(n·h), which is O(n²) for a chain-like tree.

approaches.name: Bottom-up heights with an early stop
approaches.idea: Compute each node's height once from its children's heights. If any subtree is unbalanced, return −1 and pass it straight up, skipping the rest of the work.
steps: `check(t)`: return 0 for null.
`l = check(t.left)`; if −1, return −1. Same for `r = check(t.right)`.
If `|l − r| > 1`, return −1; otherwise return `1 + max(l, r)`.
The tree is balanced when `check(root) != −1`.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once and its height reused by its parent; the stack is as deep as the height.

count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree.pattern: Top-down DFS carrying the path maximum

approaches.name: Keep the whole path and scan it at every node
approaches.idea: Walk the tree keeping the list of values on the current root-to-node path. At each node, scan that list to see whether anything is larger.
steps: DFS with a `path` list: push the node's value before visiting its children and pop it afterwards.
At each node, if no value in `path` is greater than the node's value, count it.
Return the count.
approaches.why: Each node scans a path of length up to the height h: O(n²) for a chain-like tree.

approaches.name: DFS carrying the maximum so far
approaches.idea: Only the largest value on the path matters, so pass that one number down instead of the whole path.
steps: `dfs(t, maxSoFar)`: return 0 for null.
The node is good if `t.val >= maxSoFar`.
Recurse into both children with `max(maxSoFar, t.val)` and add up the counts.
Start with `dfs(root, root.val)`.
approaches.why: O(1) work per node; only the recursion stack is used.

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree.pattern: Post-order DFS: the first node where p and q come from different sides (or it is one of them)

approaches.name: Find both root-to-node paths and compare them
approaches.idea: Record the path from the root to `p` and from the root to `q`. Both paths start the same way; the last node they share is the lowest common ancestor.
steps: DFS to find the path (list of nodes) from `root` to `p`, and likewise to `q`.
Walk both paths together while the nodes are the same.
Return the last shared node.
approaches.why: Two DFS passes over the tree; each path can be up to n nodes long in a chain-like tree.

approaches.name: One recursive pass
approaches.idea: Ask each subtree "do you contain p or q?" by returning the node found (or null). The first node where both the left and right answers are non-null is the LCA; if a node is itself `p` or `q`, it is the answer for its subtree.
steps: If `root` is null, `p` or `q`, return `root`.
Recurse: `left = lca(root.left)`, `right = lca(root.right)`.
If both are non-null, `p` and `q` are on different sides: return `root`.
Otherwise return whichever one is non-null.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; the recursion stack is as deep as the tree height. Returning a node that is `p` (or `q`) handles the case where one is an ancestor of the other.

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.pattern: Divide and conquer: preorder gives the root, inorder splits left and right subtrees

approaches.name: Recursion with a linear search for the root
approaches.idea: The first preorder value is the root. Its position in the inorder list splits the inorder list into the left subtree (before it) and the right subtree (after it); the sizes tell how to split the preorder list too.
steps: `build(preStart, inStart, inEnd)`: if the inorder range is empty, return null.
The root value is `preorder[preStart]`; scan `inorder[inStart..inEnd]` for it at index `k`.
The left subtree has `k − inStart` nodes: build it from `preStart + 1` and inorder `[inStart, k − 1]`.
Build the right subtree from `preStart + 1 + leftSize` and inorder `[k + 1, inEnd]`.
approaches.why: Each of the n nodes scans its inorder range, which can be O(n) long in a skewed tree. Recursion depth is up to n.

approaches.name: Recursion with a value → inorder-index map
approaches.idea: Same divide and conquer, but a hash map from value to inorder index finds each root in O(1) (values are distinct). Consuming preorder with a single moving index removes the size arithmetic.
steps: Map every inorder value to its index; set `next = 0` (the next preorder position).
`build(lo, hi)`: if `lo > hi`, return null.
Take the root value `preorder[next++]` and its inorder index `k`.
Build the left subtree from `[lo, k − 1]` first (preorder lists the left subtree before the right), then the right from `[k + 1, hi]`.
approaches.why: Each node is created once with O(1) lookups. The map takes O(n) and the recursion is up to n deep for a skewed tree.

serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.pattern: Preorder (or level-order) traversal with explicit null markers

approaches.name: Level order (BFS) with null markers
approaches.idea: Write the tree level by level, writing `#` for each missing child, like the test format. To rebuild, read values in the same order: each node read from the queue takes the next two tokens as its children.
steps: Serialise: BFS from the root; for each dequeued node write its value and enqueue both children; for null write `#`.
Deserialise: split on commas. If the first token is `#`, the tree is empty.
Create the root and put it in a queue; for each dequeued node, the next two tokens are its left and right children (create and enqueue those that are not `#`).
approaches.why: Each node and each null marker (n + 1 of them) is written and read once. No recursion, so a 10⁵-deep chain is no problem.

approaches.name: Preorder DFS with null markers
approaches.idea: Write the root, then the left subtree, then the right subtree, with `#` for every null. Because every null is marked, preorder alone pins down the tree: reading tokens in the same order rebuilds it recursively.
steps: Serialise: `write(t)` writes `#` for null, else the value, then `write(t.left)`, `write(t.right)`.
Deserialise: keep a shared index into the tokens; `read()` takes the next token — `#` means null, otherwise make a node and set `left = read()`, `right = read()`.
approaches.why: Each node and null marker is handled once. The recursion goes as deep as the tree; the judge runs Java and Python with a large stack, but in other settings a very deep tree favours the BFS version.

binary-tree-inorder-traversal.pattern: DFS: recursion, an explicit stack, or Morris threading

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Visit the left subtree, record the node, visit the right subtree.
steps: If the node is null, return.
Recurse left, append `node.val`, recurse right.
approaches.why: Every node is visited once. The call stack grows to the tree's height h: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) for a chain.

approaches.name: Explicit stack
approaches.idea: Simulate the recursion: slide left pushing nodes, pop one, record it, then continue from its right child.
steps: Set `cur = root`. While `cur` is not null or the stack is not empty:
Push nodes while moving `cur = cur.left` until `cur` is null.
Pop a node, record it, and set `cur` to its right child.
approaches.why: Each node is pushed and popped once. This is the answer to the iterative follow-up and avoids stack-overflow risk on very deep trees in languages with small call stacks.

approaches.name: Morris traversal
approaches.idea: Instead of a stack, temporarily point the rightmost node of each left subtree back to its ancestor, so you can climb back up; remove the link on the way back.
steps: While `cur` is not null: if it has no left child, record it and go right.
Otherwise find `pre`, the rightmost node of `cur.left`. If `pre.right` is null, set it to `cur` and go left.
If `pre.right == cur` (we came back), reset `pre.right = null`, record `cur`, and go right.
approaches.why: Each edge is walked a constant number of times, so it is still linear, with no stack at all. The tree is modified during the walk but fully restored. Mention it as the O(1)-space follow-up; the stack version is easier to get right under pressure.

binary-tree-preorder-traversal.pattern: DFS: recursion, an explicit stack, or Morris threading

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Record the node, then visit the left subtree, then the right subtree.
steps: If the node is null, return.
Append `node.val`, recurse left, recurse right.
approaches.why: One visit per node; the call stack holds one frame per level of the tree.

approaches.name: Explicit stack
approaches.idea: Pop a node, record it, and push its right child and then its left child so the left one comes out first.
steps: Push the root (if any).
While the stack is not empty: pop a node and record it.
Push its right child, then its left child.
approaches.why: Each node is pushed and popped once. Pushing right before left is the whole trick: the stack is last-in, first-out.

approaches.name: Morris traversal
approaches.idea: Same threading as Morris inorder, but record a node the first time you reach it (when creating the thread) rather than when you return.
steps: While `cur` is not null: if it has no left child, record it and go right.
Otherwise find `pre`, the rightmost node of `cur.left`. If `pre.right` is null, record `cur`, set `pre.right = cur` and go left.
If `pre.right == cur`, remove the thread and go right.
approaches.why: Linear time with no stack, and the tree is restored by the end. The only change from inorder is where the value is recorded.

binary-tree-postorder-traversal.pattern: DFS: recursion, reversed modified preorder, or one stack with a last-visited pointer

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Visit the left subtree, then the right subtree, then record the node.
steps: If the node is null, return.
Recurse left, recurse right, append `node.val`.
approaches.why: One visit per node; the call stack holds one frame per level.

approaches.name: Reverse of "node, right, left"
approaches.idea: Postorder (left, right, node) read backwards is (node, right, left), a preorder with the children swapped. Produce that with a stack and reverse it.
steps: Push the root. While the stack is not empty, pop a node and record it.
Push its left child, then its right child (so right is popped first).
Reverse the recorded list.
approaches.why: Simple and popular. The output is built in reverse, so it keeps all values before returning; the stack itself is O(h).

approaches.name: One stack with a last-visited pointer
approaches.idea: Walk like inorder, but before recording a node check whether its right subtree is finished. Remember the last recorded node to tell whether you are coming back from the right.
steps: Slide left from `cur`, pushing nodes. Peek the top node `n`.
If `n.right` exists and is not the last recorded node, move `cur = n.right` and repeat.
Otherwise pop `n`, record it, and set `last = n`.
approaches.why: Values come out in true postorder, so nothing is reversed, and the stack never holds more than one path. This is the variant to reach for when each node must be processed only after both children, such as freeing memory.

subtree-of-another-tree.pattern: Tree equality at every node (or serialise + string matching)

approaches.name: Compare at every node
approaches.idea: For each node of `root`, check whether the tree starting there is identical to `subRoot`.
steps: Write `same(a, b)`: both null → true; one null or values differ → false; otherwise compare left with left and right with right.
`isSubtree(node)` is false for a null node; otherwise `same(node, subRoot)` or `isSubtree(node.left)` or `isSubtree(node.right)`.
approaches.why: m and n are the sizes of the two trees: each of m starting nodes may compare up to n nodes. In practice most comparisons fail at the first value. h is the height of `root` (recursion depth).

approaches.name: Serialise both, then KMP
approaches.idea: Write each tree in preorder with a marker for every null child and a separator before every value. A subtree of `root` is then exactly a substring of its serialisation, found in linear time with KMP.
steps: Serialise in preorder: for a node append `,` + value, then recurse; for null append `,#`.
Build the KMP failure table for the `subRoot` string.
Scan the `root` string with KMP; return `true` if the pattern is found.
approaches.why: The leading separator stops "2" from matching inside "12", and the null markers pin down the shape, so substring ⇔ subtree. KMP guarantees linear time (a library `contains` might be quadratic in the worst case). Hashing each subtree (Merkle-style) is another linear option.

construct-quad-tree.pattern: Divide and conquer on quarters (merge uniform children)

approaches.name: Top-down: scan, then split
approaches.idea: For each square, scan all its cells. If they are all equal it is a leaf; otherwise split into four quarters and recurse.
steps: build(r, c, size): check whether every cell in the square equals `grid[r][c]`.
If so, return a leaf with that value.
Otherwise return an inner node whose children are build on the four quarters of size `size / 2`.
approaches.why: Every level of the recursion may rescan all n² cells, and there are log n levels. The recursion depth is log n (output nodes not counted).

approaches.name: Bottom-up: build quarters, then merge
approaches.idea: Build the four quarters first. If they are all leaves with the same value, the square is uniform and becomes one leaf; otherwise it is an inner node over those four.
steps: build(r, c, size): a 1 × 1 square is a leaf with `grid[r][c]`.
Otherwise build the four quarters of size `size / 2`.
If all four are leaves with equal values, return one leaf with that value; else return an inner node with the four as children.
approaches.why: Each cell is read once at the bottom and every node is created with O(1) work, so the total is linear in the number of cells. Prefix sums over the grid are another way to test a square in O(1).

delete-leaves-with-a-given-value.pattern: Postorder DFS: fix the children, then decide about the node

approaches.name: Repeat single passes until nothing changes
approaches.idea: Delete the current target leaves in one pass, then repeat, because deletions can create new target leaves.
steps: Write a pass that removes every node that is currently a leaf with value `target`, and reports whether anything was removed.
Run passes until one removes nothing (or the root itself was removed).
approaches.why: Each pass is O(n), and a chain of target values of length h needs h passes, one level per pass. The postorder version gets the chain reaction for free in a single pass.

approaches.name: Postorder recursion
approaches.idea: Clean both subtrees first and reattach the results. Only then can you tell whether the node itself has become a target leaf.
steps: If `root` is null, return null.
Set `root.left = removeLeafNodes(root.left)` and `root.right = removeLeafNodes(root.right)`.
If both children are now null and `root.val == target`, return null; otherwise return `root`.
approaches.why: Every node is visited once, and children are always settled before their parent, so a chain of target values collapses upwards in the same pass. h is the tree height (recursion depth).
